unit.title: Perform weld in flat and horizontal positions using flux cored arc welding process (FCAW)

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What does the flux inside a flux-cored wire do?
options: It makes the wire stiff so that it feeds without bending
It insulates the wire so that it cannot give a shock
It lubricates the liner so that the wire slides easily
It protects the weld pool and forms a slag on the bead

questions.stem: What is the main difference between self-shielded and gas-shielded flux-cored wire?
options: Self-shielded wire must always be used with pure argon gas
Self-shielded wire needs no gas cylinder; the other does
Gas-shielded wire makes no slag and needs no cleaning
Gas-shielded wire is only used for welding aluminium

questions.stem: Why is self-shielded flux-cored wire often chosen for site work outdoors?
options: Wind does not blow its shielding away as easily
It makes no fume at all, so no ventilation is needed
It can only be used outdoors because it needs fresh air
It gives no spatter and leaves no slag to clean off

questions.stem: Compared with solid-wire MIG, what is a main advantage of flux-cored welding on thicker plate?
options: It needs no PPE because the slag blocks the arc light
It never needs the slag removed between passes
It lays down more weld metal faster, with good penetration
It works with no electric current at all

questions.stem: Why does flux-cored welding need extra care with fume control, compared with solid-wire MIG?
options: It uses a lower current, so the fume stays in the booth
Its fume is harmless, so only the noise needs controlling
The flux in the wire makes much more smoke and fume
It needs a fan blowing straight onto the arc to work

questions.stem: Which is the best way to control fume when flux-cored welding at the Centre?
options: Use extraction at the arc and keep your head out of the plume
Weld faster, so the smoke has less time to build up
Wear a paper dust mask over the nose only
Close the booth doors to keep the smoke in one place

questions.stem: Why must safety glasses be worn under the helmet when cleaning a flux-cored weld?
options: To make the arc look brighter when you weld
Slag can fly off hot and hit the eyes when it is chipped
To stop fumes from the weld reaching the lungs
Because the helmet filter only protects the ears

questions.stem: A trainee wants to weld outside while standing on a wet floor after rain. What should happen?
options: Carry on, as flux-cored wire is safe in the wet
Carry on, but turn the current up to dry the area
Put a sheet of steel on the floor and stand on that
Stop, and weld only from a dry place in dry PPE

questions.stem: Flux-cored welding throws out a lot of spatter. What must be done about anything nearby that can burn?
options: Leave it, as flux-cored spatter is too cool to start a fire
Move it away, or cover it with a fire-resistant blanket
Wet it with oil so that it will not catch light
Cover it with a plastic sheet or a cardboard box

questions.stem: Which polarity do most gas-shielded flux-cored wires, such as E71T-1, use?
options: Direct current electrode positive (DCEP)
Direct current electrode negative (DCEN)
Alternating current (AC)
Either polarity, as it makes no difference

questions.stem: Many self-shielded flux-cored wires run on DCEN. How do you make sure the polarity is right for the wire you are using?
options: Try both ways and use the one that sounds quieter
Use DCEP for every wire, as all wire machines need it
Ask the store clerk which way round it should go
Check the wire maker's label or data sheet

questions.stem: On many small flux-cored machines, how is the polarity changed?
options: Turn the voltage knob fully up and then back down
Swap the gas hose to the other side of the machine
Switch off, then swap the leads on the polarity terminals
Fit a bigger contact tip to the gun

questions.stem: Which drive rolls are normally used for flux-cored wire?
options: Knurled rolls that grip without crushing the wire
Smooth U-groove rolls, the type made for soft aluminium wire
Flat rolls with no groove at all
Any rolls, tightened as hard as they will go

questions.stem: Why must the drive roll pressure not be set too tight on flux-cored wire?
options: Too much pressure makes the wire feed much faster than set
The hollow wire can be crushed, and flux can spill out
Tight rolls turn the machine from DC to AC
It stops the shielding gas reaching the gun

questions.stem: In the classification E71T-1, what does the "T" tell you?
options: The wire is for thin sheet only
The wire must be used with a TIG torch
The weld must be tested before use
The wire is tubular, with flux inside

questions.stem: A flux-cored wire is marked E70T-1. What does the "0" straight after the 7 tell you?
options: The wire contains no flux at all
The wire gives no spatter at all in any position
It is for flat and horizontal welding only
It needs no current when welding

questions.stem: A gas-shielded flux-cored wire is marked E71T-1C. What does the "C" tell you?
options: It must be used with a ceramic nozzle
It is made to be used with carbon dioxide gas
It can only be used for welding cast iron
It must be stored in a cold room or a refrigerator

questions.stem: Which shielding gases are normally used with gas-shielded flux-cored wire on mild steel?
options: Carbon dioxide, or an argon and carbon dioxide mix
Oxygen and acetylene, as in gas welding
Pure helium, the same gas that is used for welding copper
Natural gas taken from the workshop gas supply

questions.stem: Why must flux-cored wire be kept dry, especially in Jamaica's humid weather?
options: Damp wire is heavier, so the spool turns too slowly
Damp wire carries less current and needs higher voltage
The flux can take in moisture and cause porosity
Damp wire makes the helmet lens fog up

questions.stem: A spool of flux-cored wire will not be used for a week. How should it be kept?
options: Left on the machine with the cover open to air it
On the floor near the door, where it is cool
In a bucket with a damp cloth over the top
Sealed in its bag in a dry place, as the maker says

questions.stem: When should the contact tip on a flux-cored gun be changed?
options: When its hole is worn oval or it is blocked with spatter
Only once a year at the service, whether it is worn or not
Every time the wire spool is turned over
Whenever the gas cylinder is changed

questions.stem: Before welding, you find a cut in the insulation of the gun cable. What should you do?
options: Wrap it in masking tape and carry on welding
Stop, tag the gun out of use and report it
Carry on, but keep the cable off the floor
Turn the current down until the job is done

questions.stem: On a flux-cored machine, what does increasing the wire feed speed mainly do?
options: It lowers the current and the heat
It changes the polarity to DCEN
It raises the current and the heat
It makes the gas flow faster

questions.stem: What usually happens if the voltage is set too high for a self-shielded flux-cored wire?
options: The wire stubs into the plate and the arc stops
The bead becomes tall and narrow with no spatter
The arc becomes too short to see
A long arc with spatter and a risk of porosity

questions.stem: Which document gives the voltage, wire speed and stick-out recommended for a particular flux-cored wire?
options: The machine's sales receipt
The wire maker's data sheet or label
The Centre's attendance and time register
The gas cylinder's delivery note

questions.stem: Which gun technique is normally used for flux-cored welding, because of the slag?
options: Drag (pull), pointing back at the weld
Push, pointing ahead of the weld pool
Holding the gun still and not moving
Weaving in large circles across the plate

questions.stem: Why does the drag technique suit welding wires that make slag?
options: It stops the wire from melting too fast
It keeps the gun cooler because it is further away
It makes the slag thicker, so the weld is stronger
It stops slag running ahead and being trapped

questions.stem: Compared with short-circuit MIG with solid wire, what stick-out does flux-cored welding usually use?
options: No stick-out at all, with the contact tip touching the plate
A shorter stick-out, about 1–2 mm
A longer stick-out, as the wire maker states
Exactly the same, whatever the wire

questions.stem: For the first pass of a fillet weld on a tee joint in the horizontal position (2F), where should the wire be aimed?
options: At the top edge of the upright plate
Straight down onto the bottom plate, away from the joint
Into the root, at about 45°, slightly towards the bottom plate
Anywhere, as the slag will fill the joint

questions.stem: In a multi-pass flux-cored weld, what must be done before each new pass?
options: Cool the weld in a bucket of water so that it is easy to touch
Chip and brush off all the slag from the pass before
Grind the whole weld flat to the plate
Change the polarity for the next pass

questions.stem: How should you finish a flux-cored bead at the end of a joint?
options: Pause briefly to fill the crater before releasing the trigger
Speed up sharply and pull the gun away while still pressing the trigger
Stop suddenly and leave a deep crater
Keep welding past the end of the plate onto the bench

questions.stem: In the horizontal fillet position (2F), why can the weld end up with uneven legs?
options: The arc is weaker on the bottom plate
The slag pulls the weld up the upright plate
The upright plate always melts faster because it is cooler at the top
Gravity pulls the molten metal down onto the bottom plate

questions.stem: What does the position code "1G" mean?
options: A fillet weld in the flat position
A groove (butt) weld in the flat position
A groove weld in the vertical-up position
A fillet weld made in the overhead position

questions.stem: The flux can deal with a little dirt. Why should heavy mill scale and rust still be ground off before welding?
options: Mill scale makes the plate too hard to cut afterwards
Rust stops the work clamp gripping the bench
Ground plate is lighter and so easier to handle
Heavy scale and rust can still cause porosity and poor fusion

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of bevelling the edges of thick plate for a butt weld?
options: To make the joint look neater when it is painted over later
To use less filler wire on the job
To let the weld reach the full thickness of the plate
To stop the plates from rusting

questions.stem: Which helps to control distortion when welding a long fillet joint?
options: Tack well and weld short runs in a balanced order
Weld the whole length in one long, very slow, very hot pass
Use no tacks so that the plates can move freely
Cool each run quickly with a wet rag or water

questions.stem: Which defect is most often caused by not removing the slag between passes?
options: Undercut at the toe
Burn-through of the root
Spatter on the plate
Slag inclusion

questions.stem: Small worm-shaped gas tracks are seen on the surface of a flux-cored weld. What is a likely cause?
options: The plate was cleaned to bright metal first
A wrong stick-out, damp wire or poor gas cover
Using knurled drive rolls made for flux-cored wire
Wearing a helmet with too dark a filter shade

questions.stem: Where does undercut usually appear on a horizontal (2F) fillet weld, and why?
options: On the bottom plate, because the wire was aimed too low
In the root of the joint, because the gap was set too wide
On the upright plate, from too much heat or a wrong angle
On the back of the plate, from too little current

questions.stem: On a 2F fillet, weld metal has rolled onto the bottom plate without fusing (overlap). What is a usual cause?
options: Travel too slow, or the wire aimed too low
Too much voltage and too fast a travel
The plate was too clean and too dry
The slag was removed too soon after welding

questions.stem: How should the slag be removed so that a flux-cored weld can be inspected?
options: Leave it on, as the inspector can see through it
Pour water on it so that it cracks and falls off
Grind the whole weld away and look at the plate
Chip it off wearing eye protection, then wire brush

questions.stem: Which tool is used to check that a fillet weld is the size the drawing asks for?
options: A try square
A fillet weld gauge
A spirit level
A centre punch and hammer

questions.stem: On a flux-cored fillet weld, which of these is a sign of good work?
options: Slag still stuck in the ripples all along the length of the bead
A tall, narrow bead with sharp edges at the toes
Even ripples, equal legs and smooth toes with no holes
Heavy spatter and worm marks along the face

questions.stem: What should be done with wire offcuts and slag at the end of the job?
options: Sweep them up and put them in the metal scrap bin
Leave them on the floor to cool overnight
Throw them out of the window into the yard
Put them in the paper bin with the rags

questions.stem: During a job the wire keeps stopping and starting. What should you do?
options: Pull the wire through the gun by hand while the trigger is pressed
Turn the voltage fully up and carry on
Hit the wire feeder with a hammer until it runs
Stop, switch off and check the feed, or report it

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Compare self-shielded and gas-shielded flux-cored welding. Give the main differences and say when you would choose each.
essays.modelAnswer: Both processes use a hollow, tubular wire filled with flux, fed from a spool through a gun, and both leave a slag on the weld that must be removed. Self-shielded wire makes all of its own shielding from the flux, so no gas cylinder is needed. Many self-shielded wires run on DCEN. It is good for site work outdoors, because wind does not blow its shield away as easily, and the equipment is simple to carry. It makes more fume and spatter, and the weld can be less smooth. Gas-shielded wire uses the flux plus a shielding gas, usually carbon dioxide or an argon and carbon dioxide mix, and most of these wires run on DCEP. It gives a smoother arc, less spatter, good penetration and a better-looking weld, so it is often used in the workshop on thicker plate. It needs a gas cylinder and must be screened from draughts. For either type, check the wire maker's label for the polarity, settings and gas.
markingPoints: Both use a tubular, flux-filled wire and leave a slag
Self-shielded: no gas cylinder, many run on DCEN, good outdoors and on site
Gas-shielded: carbon dioxide or argon/CO2 mix, most run on DCEP, smoother arc and less spatter
Gas-shielded needs a cylinder and shelter from draughts; self-shielded makes more fume and spatter
Checks the wire maker's label for polarity, settings and gas

essays.stem: Flux-cored welding makes a lot of fume. Explain why the fume is harmful, and describe how a welder at the Centre should protect themselves and others.
essays.modelAnswer: Flux-cored welding gives off much more smoke and fume than solid-wire MIG, because the flux inside the wire burns in the arc. The fume is made of tiny particles of metal oxides and flux, and the arc also makes gases such as ozone and carbon monoxide. Breathing it can cause coughing, headaches, a sore throat and metal fume fever, and over many years it can damage the lungs and nerves. To control it, use local exhaust ventilation with the hood close to the arc, drawing the fume away from the face, and check that it is switched on and working before you start. Keep your head to the side, out of the rising plume. Weld in a ventilated booth with screens, so that others are not in the fume or the arc light. Clean off paint, oil and zinc coatings before welding. Where extraction cannot keep the fume down, wear a suitable respirator that fits well. Read the safety data sheet for the wire and follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: The burning flux makes more fume: metal oxide particles plus gases such as ozone and carbon monoxide
Gives short-term and long-term health effects
Local exhaust ventilation close to the arc, switched on and working
Head out of the plume; booth and screens; coatings removed first
Respirator where needed; safety data sheet, maker's instructions and Centre rules

essays.stem: Describe how you would set up a flux-cored welding machine for a new job, from choosing the wire to the first test bead.
essays.modelAnswer: First read the drawing and the welding procedure to find the wire type and size, the plate thickness and the position. Check the wire label to see whether it is self-shielded or gas-shielded and which polarity it needs. With the machine switched off and isolated, set the polarity by connecting the gun and work leads to the correct terminals, for example DCEP for most gas-shielded wires or DCEN for many self-shielded wires. Fit knurled drive rolls of the right size, load the spool, feed the wire into the rolls and set the pressure just enough to feed without crushing the wire. Feed the wire through the gun with the tip removed, keeping the gun pointed away from people, then fit the right contact tip and nozzle. For gas-shielded wire, fit the regulator and set the gas flow. Fix the work clamp on clean metal close to the weld. Set the voltage and wire speed from the maker's chart, weld a test bead on scrap of the same thickness and adjust until the arc is smooth and the bead is well fused.
markingPoints: Reads the procedure, drawing and wire label (type, size, polarity)
Sets the correct polarity with the machine switched off
Fits knurled drive rolls at the right pressure, and the correct contact tip
Sets the gas flow for gas-shielded wire; work clamp on clean metal near the weld
Takes settings from the maker's chart and adjusts after a test bead on scrap

essays.stem: Describe how to make a three-pass fillet weld on a tee joint in the horizontal position (2F) with flux-cored wire, including the gun angles and the cleaning between passes.
essays.modelAnswer: Clean the plates to bright metal and tack the upright plate square on the base plate. Set the machine from the wire maker's chart and test on scrap. For the first (root) pass, aim the wire into the root of the joint at about 45° between the plates, with a drag angle of about 10–20° back towards the finished weld, and keep the stick-out steady at the length the maker gives. Travel at an even speed so that the bead fuses into both plates. Chip off all the slag and wire brush the bead, wearing safety glasses. Lay the second pass along the bottom plate, aimed at the lower toe of the first pass, so that it covers about half of it. Clean off the slag again. Lay the third pass along the upright plate, aimed at the upper toe of the second pass, so that it fills the rest of the joint and blends into the upright plate without undercut. Fill the crater at the end of each pass. Remove all the slag, then check for equal legs of the right size and no undercut, overlap, porosity or slag.
markingPoints: Plates cleaned and tacked square; settings from the chart and tested on scrap
Root pass at about 45° into the root, with a drag angle and a steady stick-out
All slag removed between every pass, with eye protection
Second pass along the bottom plate, third along the upright plate, each overlapping correctly
Craters filled; finished weld checked for equal legs and defects

essays.stem: Explain why flux-cored wire must be stored and handled correctly, and describe how to do this at the Centre.
essays.modelAnswer: The flux inside a flux-cored wire can take in moisture from the air, and Jamaica's warm, humid weather makes this worse. Damp flux can cause porosity, worm tracks and hydrogen in the weld, which can lead to cracking. Dirt or rust on the wire can also cause poor feeding and porosity, and a dented or crushed wire will not feed smoothly. So keep new spools sealed in their original bags and boxes until they are needed, and store them in a clean, dry store room, off the floor and away from water, steam and sea air. Keep the label with the spool so that the wire type and batch are known. When a spool is on the machine, keep the feeder cover closed, and if it will not be used for a few days, put it back in a sealed bag, as the maker advises. Handle spools carefully so that they are not dropped or dented, and use the oldest stock first. Do not use wire that is rusty or wet; report it to the instructor.
markingPoints: The flux takes in moisture, especially in humid weather
Effects: porosity, worm tracks, hydrogen cracking, poor feeding
Kept sealed in its packing in a clean, dry place off the floor
Feeder cover closed; spools not in use put back in a sealed bag; label kept
Handled with care, oldest used first; rusty or wet wire not used and reported

essays.stem: Name four defects that can be found in flux-cored welds. For each one, give a cause and a way to prevent it.
essays.modelAnswer: Slag inclusion is slag trapped inside the weld. It is caused by not cleaning all the slag off between passes, or by pushing the gun so that slag runs ahead of the pool. Prevent it by chipping and brushing every pass and using a drag angle. Porosity, including worm tracks, is gas holes in the weld. It is caused by damp wire, a wrong stick-out, too high a voltage, poor gas cover with gas-shielded wire, or dirty plate. Prevent it by storing wire dry, keeping the stick-out the maker gives, setting the voltage correctly and cleaning the plate. Lack of fusion is weld metal that has not melted into the plate or into the pass before. It is caused by too little heat, the wrong travel speed or a wrong angle. Prevent it with correct settings and by keeping the arc on the leading edge of the pool. Undercut is a groove along the toe on the upright plate, caused by too much voltage or a wrong angle; prevent it with the right settings and angle.
markingPoints: Names four real FCAW defects (for example slag inclusion, porosity or worm tracks, lack of fusion, undercut, overlap)
Gives a correct cause for each
Gives a correct way to prevent each
Links the causes to slag cleaning, wire storage, settings and technique

essays.stem: Explain what welding polarity is, why it matters in flux-cored welding, and how to change it safely.
essays.modelAnswer: Polarity is the way the welding leads are connected to the positive and negative terminals of a direct current machine. With DCEP (direct current electrode positive) the gun lead is on the positive terminal and the work lead on the negative. With DCEN (direct current electrode negative) it is the other way round. Polarity matters because it changes where the heat goes and how the flux works. Most gas-shielded flux-cored wires are made to run on DCEP, while many self-shielded wires run on DCEN. With the wrong polarity the arc is unstable, there is much more spatter, penetration is poor and the weld may be porous. So always read the wire label or data sheet to find the right polarity. To change it, switch the machine off and isolate it, then swap the leads on the polarity terminals and tighten them firmly, because a loose connection gets hot. Check that the work clamp is on clean metal near the weld. Then switch on and make a test bead on scrap.
markingPoints: Explains polarity as the connection of the gun and work leads to positive and negative (DCEP and DCEN)
Most gas-shielded wires run on DCEP and many self-shielded wires on DCEN: check the label
Wrong polarity gives an unstable arc, spatter, poor penetration or porosity
Switches off and isolates before changing; tightens the connections
Makes a test bead on scrap afterwards

essays.stem: Describe how you would plan and prepare the work area, equipment and materials before starting a flux-cored welding job.
essays.modelAnswer: First read the job card, drawing and welding procedure, so that you know the joint, the plate size, the wire, the position and the size of weld. Check that you have the right plate, wire, gas if it is needed, and tools such as a grinder, chipping hammer, wire brush, clamps and a fillet gauge. Prepare the work area: weld in a booth with screens, remove anything that can burn, check that a fire extinguisher is close and that the fume extraction works. Check the machine, gun, leads and clamp for damage, and set the polarity and drive rolls for the wire. Cut and clean the plate, grinding off rust, mill scale, paint and oil for about 25 mm back from the joint, because dirt causes porosity and poor fusion. Bevel the edges if the drawing asks for it. Fit the parts up square with the correct gap, and tack them so that they cannot move. Put on full PPE, warn others nearby, and make a test bead on scrap before starting the job.
markingPoints: Reads the job card, drawing and procedure for the joint, wire, position and weld size
Gathers the correct materials and tools
Prepares a safe area: screens, burnable items removed, extinguisher, working extraction
Checks the equipment and sets the polarity and drive rolls
Cleans, fits up and tacks the plate; full PPE and a test bead on scrap

essays.stem: Describe how you would inspect a finished flux-cored fillet weld, and what you would do if you found a fault.
essays.modelAnswer: First remove all the slag with a chipping hammer, wearing safety glasses, then wire brush the weld so that the surface can be seen clearly. In good light, check the size of the weld with a fillet gauge: the legs should be equal and match the drawing, and the face should not be too thin or too humped. Check the bead for an even width and ripple, and smooth blending into both plates at the toes. Look for undercut on the upright plate, overlap on the bottom plate, porosity or worm tracks, slag left in the ripples, cracks or deep craters at the end, and heavy spatter. Check the starts and stops closely. Check that the parts are still square and in line. If you find a fault, mark it with chalk, write it on the inspection sheet with the job number, and tell the instructor. Do not hide it with paint or grinding. The instructor will decide whether it can be repaired, for example by grinding it out and welding again, or whether the job must be done again.
markingPoints: Removes all slag and brushes the weld, with eye protection
Checks the size with a fillet gauge against the drawing
Checks bead shape and named defects, including the starts and stops
Checks the parts are still square and in line
Marks, records and reports faults, and does not hide them

essays.stem: Explain how voltage, wire feed speed and stick-out each affect a flux-cored weld.
essays.modelAnswer: Wire feed speed sets the current. More wire speed gives more amps, more heat, a bigger bead and deeper penetration; too little gives a small, weak weld with poor fusion. Voltage sets the arc length. If it is too high, the arc is long, the bead is wide and flat, there is more spatter, and with self-shielded wire there is a greater risk of porosity because air gets into the arc. If it is too low, the wire stubs into the plate, the arc is rough and the bead is tall and narrow. Stick-out is the length of wire between the contact tip and the arc. Flux-cored wire usually needs a longer stick-out than solid wire, as the maker states. If the stick-out is too long, the current drops, penetration is poor and the arc can wander. If it is too short, spatter builds up on the tip and nozzle, and the tip can overheat. Keep all three at the maker's settings, and check them on scrap before welding the job.
markingPoints: Wire feed speed sets the current: effect of more and less
Voltage sets the arc length: too high gives spatter, a wide bead and a risk of porosity; too low gives stubbing and a tall bead
Flux-cored wire usually needs a longer stick-out, as the maker states
Effects of a stick-out that is too long or too short
Uses the maker's settings and checks them on scrap

practical1.title: Three-pass flux-cored fillet welds on tee joints in the horizontal position (2F), 10 mm plate
practical1.brief: As a group, set up a safe flux-cored welding station and weld two tee joints in 10 mm mild steel plate with three-pass fillet welds in the horizontal position (2F), using the flux-cored wire the Centre stocks (for example 1.2 mm E71T-1 with gas, or a self-shielded wire). Together, read the wire label, set the polarity with the machine off, fit knurled drive rolls and set the gas flow if the wire needs gas. Every member makes at least one pass while the assessor watches, removes all the slag before the next pass, and takes part in checking the finished welds with a fillet gauge. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the welds are finished and the area is clean.
materials: 4 pieces of 10 mm mild steel plate, about 150 mm × 75 mm (for 2 tee joints)
Scrap plate of the same thickness for test beads
Flux-cored wire as the Centre stocks, with its label or data sheet
Shielding gas and regulator/flowmeter, if the wire is gas-shielded
Wire feed welding machine with knurled drive rolls
Chipping hammer, wire brush and fillet weld gauge
Angle grinder with flap disc (for cleaning)
photos: The welding station set up with extraction in place, and every member in full PPE
The wire label and the polarity connections on the machine
Plates cleaned and tacked square as tee joints
Root pass, with the slag removed
Second pass on the bottom plate, cleaned
Finished three-pass welds, top view and end view showing both legs
The fillet gauge on a finished weld
The work area cleaned, offcuts and slag in the scrap bin
checklist: Wore full PPE correctly throughout, including safety glasses for chipping
Read the wire label and helped set the correct polarity with the machine off
Cleaned the plates and tacked them square and in line
Used a drag angle and a steady stick-out, aimed correctly for each pass
Removed all the slag between passes
Finished fillet: equal legs to size, no undercut, overlap, porosity or slag on the surface
Checked a weld with the fillet gauge and recorded the result
Left the work area safe and tidy, with the wire covered or bagged
safety: Use the fume extraction close to the arc; flux-cored welding makes heavy fume
Weld only in a booth or behind screens so others are not exposed to arc flash
Remove anything that can burn; keep a fire extinguisher at hand
Switch off and isolate the machine before changing polarity or drive rolls
Wear safety glasses under the helmet when chipping hot slag
Treat all metal as hot: use tongs or pliers and mark hot work

practical2.title: Flux-cored single-V butt weld in the flat position (1G) on a backing strip, 10 mm plate
practical2.brief: As a group, prepare and weld a single-V butt joint in two pieces of 10 mm mild steel plate (about 150 mm × 100 mm) in the flat position (1G), on a steel backing strip, using the Centre's flux-cored wire. Bevel each edge to about 30°, set the root gap the Centre's procedure gives, and tack the plates to the backing strip in line. Weld a root pass, then fill and cap passes, removing the slag between every pass. Share the work so that every member does some of the preparation and makes at least one pass while the assessor watches. As a group, inspect the finished weld and fill in an inspection sheet. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when the weld is finished and the area is clean.
materials: 2 pieces of 10 mm mild steel plate, about 150 mm × 100 mm
Steel backing strip, about 25 mm wide and 200 mm long
Flux-cored wire as the Centre stocks, with its label or data sheet
Wire feed welding machine, with gas and regulator if needed
Angle grinder with grinding disc, bevel gauge and steel rule
photos: Bevelled edges, with the bevel gauge in place
Plates tacked on the backing strip, showing the root gap
The work area cleaned, offcuts and slag in the scrap bin
checklist: Wore full PPE correctly throughout, including a face shield and glasses when grinding
Took part in bevelling, cleaning or fitting up the plates
Set the root gap and tacked the plates in line on the backing strip
Made a pass with good fusion into both bevels and the backing strip
Removed all the slag before the next pass
Capping pass of even width and height, with no undercut or porosity
Helped inspect the weld and fill in the inspection sheet
Left the work area safe and tidy
safety: Wear a face shield and safety glasses when grinding; check the disc suits the grinder and is undamaged
Use the fume extraction close to the arc and keep your head out of the plume
Weld only in a booth or behind screens; warn others before you strike an arc
Remove anything that can burn; keep a fire extinguisher at hand
Keep gloves and clothing dry; never stand in water
Treat all metal as hot: use tongs and mark hot work
